content: In January 1991, an outbreak of cholera emerged in Peru and rapidly spread to numerous other Latin American countries. The delayed reporting of cholera cases in some regions made it difficult to fully understand the extent of the epidemic. An evaluation of cholera surveillance systems in several countries revealed recurring issues, including inconsistent case definitions, inadequate laboratory surveillance, suboptimal surveillance methods, poor national coordination, and challenges in data management. A critical conclusion was that a simple and well-communicated cholera surveillance system during an epidemic can significantly enhance prevention and treatment efforts. Cholera is a highly preventable and treatable disease. Chlorination of water supplies and the implementation of emergency measures can effectively prevent transmission. Providing timely access to oral and intravenous rehydration therapy can dramatically reduce mortality rates. Prevention and treatment efforts are most effective when there is collaboration between regional and central public health offices, as well as at national and international levels. A clear and representative understanding of the epidemic is essential for assessing its progression, determining resource needs, and evaluating the effectiveness of control measures. A straightforward and widely accepted surveillance system is the best way to achieve this understanding. When cholera first appeared in Peru in January 1991, it quickly spread to other Latin American countries. The unexpected nature of the epidemic left some countries with little time to prepare. However, many countries had already developed and implemented preparedness plans for cholera control. An ideal cholera control plan includes essential components such as health education, environmental sanitation, clinical management, laboratory diagnosis, epidemiologic investigation, and surveillance. During a cholera epidemic, surveillance is crucial for estimating incidence and fatality rates, tracking the epidemic's spread, planning the distribution of resources for treatment and prevention, conducting timely epidemiologic investigations, and evaluating the effectiveness of control measures. Investigations of the cholera epidemic in various countries identified several recurring problems with surveillance systems, including difficulties in data collection, transmission, and analysis. These issues often caused delays and obscured the epidemic's scope at regional, national, and international levels. Additionally, some national surveillance systems used overly complex case definitions, which hindered efficient and rapid reporting of cases. This report highlights selected problems in cholera surveillance systems in some Latin American countries and provides recommendations to improve cholera surveillance at both national and international levels. One common issue in cholera surveillance is the definition of cases. A case definition is a set of objective criteria (symptoms, signs, and laboratory data) that ensures reliable and reproducible reporting of the disease. Many countries use two main categories for cholera cases: suspect and confirmed. However, within these categories, multiple definitions are often used, which complicates reporting and analysis. For example, one country uses three definitions for a suspect case of cholera, including profuse diarrhea with severe dehydration in individuals over five years old, acute diarrhea in areas with confirmed cholera, and acute diarrhea in individuals who traveled through an infected area within five days before illness onset. Another country uses a single definition for a suspect case but adds a probable case category for individuals with epidemiologic links to other cholera cases. Such multiple definitions increase reporting difficulties and may confuse the analysis of surveillance data. Most countries use five years as the lower age limit for cholera surveillance, although the World Health Organization (WHO) previously recommended ten years as the lower age limit for initial identification of cholera. Changes to lower this age limit are underway, as five years corresponds to the transition from preschool to school age, a period when children may be more exposed to communicable diseases, including cholera. Using five years as the lower age limit excludes more cases of diarrhea that are not cholera, making the definition more specific. The confirmed case category is usually defined as Vibrio cholerae O1 infection verified by laboratory methods, most commonly stool culture with confirmation of the isolate as O1 V. cholerae. In rare cases, demonstrating that the isolate produces cholera toxin may be helpful, as some nontoxigenic O1 strains of V. cholerae have been documented. Simply counting laboratory isolates as cases may obscure the true picture of the epidemic. For instance, routine culturing of specimens from family members and close contacts of confirmed cholera patients in one country identified asymptomatic infections, which were then reported as confirmed cholera cases. Asymptomatic cholera infections are common during epidemics but cannot be identified as cases based solely on clinical signs and symptoms. Reporting individuals without diarrhea as confirmed cholera cases can distort surveillance data. The broad spectrum of illness associated with cholera infection presents a major challenge for simple case definitions. Over 70% of infected individuals are asymptomatic, and an additional 15%-23% have mild or moderate non-bloody diarrhea similar to diarrhea from other causes. A case definition based solely on severe dehydrating diarrhea will be more specific but will miss many infected individuals. In public health action, an accurate report of the number of symptomatic infections is more useful. No single case definition is perfect; a balance between sensitivity and specificity is needed to provide a representative picture of the epidemic in any given area. For cholera surveillance during an epidemic, case definitions should be brief and simple to facilitate uniform and rapid reporting. Cholera case definitions should be limited to two categories: confirmed and suspect. A confirmed cholera case is a laboratory-confirmed V. cholerae O1 infection in any person with diarrhea. In the epidemic setting, a suspect case of cholera should be defined as acute, watery diarrhea in a person aged five years or older. The laboratory is a central component of cholera surveillance. It is essential for confirming the presence of V. cholerae O1 in an area, monitoring its continued presence or disappearance, determining its antimicrobial susceptibilities, and identifying its presence in the environment. Preliminary isolation and confirmation of V. cholerae O1 require trained personnel using thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose (TCBS) agar and polyvalent antisera. During the current cholera epidemic in Latin America, most countries were able to staff some laboratories with trained personnel and minimal supplies shortly after the first few cholera cases were confirmed. However, as the epidemic advanced, many laboratories were quickly overwhelmed with demands for confirmation of numerous suspect cholera patients, slowing the reporting of laboratory results. In regional laboratories, trained personnel are needed to confirm V. cholerae O1 infection using TCBS agar and polyvalent antisera. At the central laboratory, trained personnel are also needed to confirm field isolates. Initially, in an area threatened with cholera, a sample of individuals with suspect cases should have specimens taken for culture. Once cholera is established in an area, stool cultures should be used only to confirm the continued presence of V. cholerae O1 and to monitor its antibiotic susceptibility. Every laboratory that identifies V. cholerae O1 should provide weekly reports of the total number of patient isolates to designated regional and central offices. In areas where cholera has not been confirmed, especially those bordering cholera-affected areas, Moore swabs can be placed in sewage effluents of sentinel towns and cities every 1-3 weeks. If V. cholerae O1 is isolated from sewage or a person in a given area, the organism's presence in the area has been established, and surveillance with Moore swabs can be discontinued. Thereafter, laboratory-based surveillance in that area should focus on patients with diarrhea. When epidemic cholera appears in a region, two stages of surveillance are observed: an early stage, when cultures are obtained from many patients with diarrhea to diagnose cholera, and a later stage, when cholera is firmly established in the region and larger numbers of people are ill. In the early stage, the number of confirmed cases may be small and may represent a minor proportion of the suspect cases. Most countries report only culture-confirmed cases at this stage. However, as the cholera epidemic grows, more cases are confirmed, and the number of patients with suspect cases more accurately reflects the cholera situation in that area. Many countries, nonetheless, continue to report only culture-confirmed cases in this later stage of cholera surveillance due to concerns about public response and adverse economic consequences if the larger number of suspect cases is reported. In a cholera-threatened area, available diarrhea surveillance data can be reviewed to detect trends suggesting early cholera outbreaks. Any report of acute dehydrating diarrhea affecting a person aged five years or older should immediately alert local public health workers to investigate for possible cholera. Early in a cholera epidemic, when small numbers of cases are being confirmed, a region may report only culture-confirmed cases. However, when the number of confirmed cases becomes sufficiently high, surveillance should shift to using the suspect case definition because it allows simpler, more timely, and more accurate reporting and avoids overburdening laboratory resources. For a region in this later stage of cholera surveillance, it may be appropriate to limit culturing to a sample of the suspect cases that should continue to be reported. The decision as to when the number of confirmed cases becomes sufficiently high to change from reporting only confirmed cases to reporting cases in both suspect and confirmed categories should be made promptly on an individual basis after all implications have been assessed. Since most cholera outbreaks are large and often well established when confirmed, early shifting to reporting suspect cases may be more appropriate. When the cholera epidemic wanes and the number of infections decreases to the level of the early stage of the epidemic, some countries may revert to reporting only confirmed cases. However, in many areas, cholera appears seasonally, with numbers of cases increasing in warm months and decreasing in cold months. Therefore, it may be useful to report suspect cases for at least a year after the epidemic wanes until it is clearly shown that cholera is controlled in an area. At that time, it is reasonable to return to reporting only confirmed cases for that area. Some countries have administered lengthy, detailed questionnaires to every patient with cholera. While detailed information may be helpful in describing a sample of cholera cases clinically, it is of epidemiologic interest only in the earliest phase of an epidemic. Thereafter, as the number of cholera cases increases, the forms may be incomplete or ignored, and much of the data will be unmanageable and unanalyzed unless data-handling resources are diverted from other worthwhile programs. Exposure information collected from patients alone will not determine the modes of transmission, as cholera may be transmitted by common foods or beverages or by multiple sources that vary from place to place. Well-designed and well-administered case-control investigations in affected areas are a more effective approach to identifying vehicles of transmission. In summary, lengthy surveillance questionnaires waste scarce human resources and impede the handling of surveillance data. For cholera, exposure histories are best reserved for investigations. Surveillance should be streamlined, using simple case definitions and concentrating on timely and accurate reporting of data. At the local level, including all treatment centers, information gathered about patients who meet the cholera surveillance case definition should be basic, including age, gender, date treated, and home address. The information transmitted to regional and central levels may include age, gender, and location, but it should primarily focus on the numbers of cases, hospitalized patients, and deaths. Surveillance and laboratory information is of little value unless it is communicated clearly and promptly. Timely reporting of laboratory results to a regional epidemiology office will allow early identification of cholera-affected areas and permit immediate investigations. Timely reporting to the central laboratory will allow early confirmation of the isolates. To complete the information loop, timely feedback to the original submitter of the isolates will help validate diagnoses and improve patient care. Similarly, timely reporting of the total number of cases and basic analysis results from a central epidemiology office back to the laboratories and regional epidemiology offices is essential to characterize the epidemic and ensure continued cooperation at all levels. In some locations, information dissemination among these major components in the surveillance process has not always been timely and complete. Early in the cholera epidemic in Latin America, for example, some countries instituted emergency daily reporting of the number of cases to a central office but did not communicate the total and cumulative number of cases by region to their constituents until months later. The suitable form of information flow among local and central levels must be worked out country by country. A proposed communication system includes both reporting to a central office and feedback to regional offices. Rapid methods (e.g., radio, telephone, telegram) should be used to report the number of suspect cases, the number of confirmed cases, the number of patients who were hospitalized, and the number who died. A rapid switch to weekly reporting will often reduce the burden of work created by daily reporting without compromising the main goals of surveillance. The administrative level to which each treatment center's report should be sent must be clearly identified. Surveillance data should be analyzed promptly and frequently. Basic tabulation and comparison of data should be performed at the local and regional levels if trained personnel are available. At the central level, epidemiologists should analyze reports of suspect and confirmed cholera cases by region and by week to track the spread of the epidemic, determine whether unexpectedly large numbers of cases are occurring in any region, and evaluate the impact of interventions. The results should be disseminated to all levels and used to estimate resources needed at local levels and to decide whether epidemiologic investigations are needed. When surveillance data suggest an increase in the number of cases in an area, an epidemiologic investigation should be conducted to determine the modes of transmission and identify further prevention measures. The results of these investigations should be reported to all categories of participants in the surveillance system. Cholera is one of three internationally notifiable diseases, and countries are requested to report cases to WHO promptly. Some governments may be concerned that reporting a large number of cases could negatively impact economic factors such as tourism and food exportation. However, prompt and accurate reporting will improve national and international efforts to allocate resources to control cholera morbidity and mortality. The number of cholera cases should be reported to WHO in a timely manner.
